ch10.title: The Crisis at Capernaum
ch10.b002: From the Friday evening they came back to Bethsaida, the Master was silent. All twelve could tell he was turning over something heavy. On the Sabbath morning he ate no breakfast and hardly touched his food at noon. The apostles and their associates drifted about in small knots—in the house, in the garden, along the shore. An uneasy waiting, the dread of not knowing what was coming, lay over the whole house like a mist. Since they had left Jerusalem the Master had said very little to them.
ch10.b003: The Alpheus twins did not feel that mist quite as the others did. Or rather, they felt it, but they had no name for it. They had risen early and swept the yard. A great many people would come to the synagogue that afternoon, and the way would need to be kept clear. Handling crowds was their work, and they were faithful to it. The synagogue would be full today. The twins took that to be a good thing: when many people came, the Master would be glad. Their reckoning was as simple as that, and thanks to its simplicity they were, that morning, the most at ease of all the twelve.
ch10.b004: The others’ faces were different. As they swept, the twins picked up scraps of what was said. Peter was depressed, if not quite downcast. Andrew did not know what to do for his dejected companions. Nathaniel said they were in the lull before the storm. Thomas thought something out of the ordinary was about to happen. Philip told David Zebedee to forget about plans for feeding and lodging the crowds until they knew what the Master was thinking. Matthew was hurrying about again, trying to fill up the treasury. James and John speculated back and forth about what the afternoon’s sermon in the synagogue would be like. Simon Zelotes said the Father in heaven might be about to step in in some unexpected way to stand by his Son. It was less a belief than a hope.
ch10.b005: And Judas Iscariot was nursing a thought he did not speak aloud to anyone. He felt it was a little daring even to entertain it. Perhaps the Master was regretting now that he had lacked the courage and the nerve to let the five thousand proclaim him king of the Jews. Judas set the thought down in a corner of his mind the way he might jot a note in the margin of his ledger. If so, it was not too late. Today, in the synagogue, before the men who had come down from Jerusalem—at last.
ch10.b006: When Nathaniel’s phrase about the lull before the storm drifted across the yard, Judas frowned. The man was playing with words even on a day like this. The apostolic company stood at a crossroads, and he was talking about the weather. Judas had long thought that Nathaniel did not take his apostleship seriously enough. Today that thought pricked him again like a small thorn. He said nothing about it to anyone. Not yet.
ch10.b007: A little after noon the Master left the house for the synagogue. The apostles fell in silently behind him. Just then one of the twins set down his broom and came up to him with a beaming face. We pray the Father will help you, he said, and that we may have bigger crowds than ever. It was the greeting of a man who suspected nothing. The Master looked at him. What passed through his eyes, the twin could not read. He knew only that the Master had looked at him. That was enough to make him happy, and his brother was happy too. Judas Iscariot watched and gave a slight twist of the mouth. Simple souls. He did not notice that the greeting was not so very different from his own thought.
ch10.b009: At three o’clock the new synagogue at Capernaum was packed. Jairus presided. The day before, fifty-three Pharisees and Sadducees had come down from Jerusalem, and more than thirty leaders of the neighboring synagogues were there as well. They came under direct orders from the Sanhedrin—the orthodox vanguard, sent to open the war in the open. Beside them, in the seats of honor, sat observers from Herod Antipas, sent to find out whether it was true that, over in his brother Philip’s domains, the people had tried to proclaim Jesus king.
ch10.b010: Judas Iscariot stood by a pillar near the door and took stock of the room. Faces from Jerusalem, faces from Herod’s court, faces from Capernaum. He weighed them. One word from the Master here today, and the scales might tip. He had heard that from Friday evening right through the Sabbath morning the Jerusalem men had pressed Jairus to keep the Master from speaking. Jairus had given them only one answer: he had granted the request, and he would not break his word. Judas looked at Jairus again. If the ruler of the synagogue would stand as firm as that, there was a chance.
ch10.b011: The Master opened Deuteronomy and read a fearful passage: if the people would not hearken to the voice of God, the curses would overtake them; they would fall before their enemies, and they and the king they had set over themselves would be handed over to a strange nation. Then he read from Jeremiah—how the priests and teachers had seized the prophet who warned that the house would be made like Shiloh, and cried out that he must die. Then the Master looked up and asked them what the leaders of this people would do today with a man who warned them of the day of their spiritual doom. The room went rigid.
ch10.b012: A chill ran down Judas’s spine. These were not the words he had been waiting for. What new sign were they looking for from him? the Master asked. They already had evidence enough to decide. Like Joshua, he said, they must choose this day whom they would serve. And some of them, when they could not find him after the feeding, had hired the Tiberias fishing boats that had taken shelter nearby from a storm, and come chasing after him—for what? Not for truth, but for more bread they had not worked for. They should seek not the food that perishes but the food that leads to eternal life.
ch10.b013: Then the Master raised his hand and pointed to the lintel above the synagogue door. Carved in the stone was a pot of manna, wreathed in clusters of grapes. What their fathers ate in the wilderness, he said, was not bread from heaven but bread of the earth. Now the Father was ready to give them the true bread of life. And then he said it: “⟦Q 153:2.8⟧I am this bread of life.⟦/Q⟧” Whoever came to him would not hunger, and whoever believed him would never thirst. Yesterday he had fed them with bread for their bodies; today he offered them the bread of life for their hungry souls.
ch10.b014: Judas looked up at that stone pot. He had seen the carving dozens of times. Today, for the first time, it looked like a gravestone. Bread for five thousand. That had been the largest pledge he had staked on this whole venture. And now the Master was marking that pledge down, himself, in front of everyone. That bread had been bread of the earth, he was saying; you came for your stomachs. It was the sound of a man kicking away the steps to a throne one at a time.
ch10.b015: A teacher from Jerusalem, a member of the Sanhedrin, stood up. Did he understand rightly that the Master claimed to be bread come down from heaven, and that the manna Moses gave their fathers was not? The Master said he had understood rightly. Then the man asked: was this not Jesus of Nazareth, son of Joseph the carpenter? Did they not know his father and mother, his brothers and sisters? How could he say he had come down from heaven? A murmur rose through the synagogue. The Master stood up and asked them to be patient; truth never suffers from honest examination. He was all they said, he told them, and more. The Father and he were one.
ch10.b016: When he finished, the ruler of the synagogue dismissed the congregation, but no one left. Judas stood with his back against the pillar. And it was then that a sentence took clear shape inside him for the first time. I could leave this man. The sentence startled him. His heart lurched. He shoved it back down. No. Not yet. This too must be some kind of calculation. Had the Master not always seen a move further ahead than the rest of them? He put the sentence into the deepest drawer of his mind and locked it. For a while afterward he lived as though he had forgotten the drawer existed. But the drawer was there.
ch10.b018: The after meeting went on for more than three hours. Questions poured in. A few came from bewildered disciples, but most were thrown by men who wanted only to trap him. Peter stood close by the Master and took each question as though it struck his own body. He looked at the faces around him. Faces that a month ago had shouted king in the park now stood here with folded arms. The turn had come so fast it made Peter dizzy.
ch10.b019: One of the Pharisees from Jerusalem climbed up on a lampstand and shouted down: if the Master was the bread of life, how could he give them his flesh to eat and his blood to drink? What use was a teaching that could not be carried out? Laughter broke out. The Master answered calmly that he had never taught that his flesh was bread or his blood water. He had said that his life in the flesh was a bestowal of the bread of heaven. They could not eat his flesh, but they could become one with him in spirit, as he was one in spirit with the Father.
ch10.b020: One of the spies broke in. They had noticed, he said, that neither the Master nor his apostles washed their hands properly before eating bread; why did they disregard the tradition of the elders? The Master turned the question back on him. Why did they break the commandment of God for the sake of their tradition? The commandment said to honor father and mother—yet had they not made a rule that let a man off that duty merely by declaring that the money which might have helped his parents had been given to God? Then, speaking to everyone, he said that what defiles a man is not what goes into his mouth but what comes out of his heart.
ch10.b021: Peter’s ears burned. The washing of hands was bred into his bones too. He went to the Master and asked in a low voice whether he would explain those words, so that his hearers would not be needlessly offended. The Master looked at him and asked whether he too was so slow to understand. Peter’s face went hot. The rebuke was gentle, but it found its mark. The Master explained that if the blind lead the blind, both fall into the pit; that it is from the heart that evil thoughts come, and murder and theft, jealousy and pride and false witness. Peter nodded. But that night, lying in bed, he went over and over those few words: are you also so slow? He was slow. That was the truth. And still the Master kept this slow man at his side.
ch10.b022: Then one of the Pharisees brought forward a distraught young man, tormented and thrashing. Could the Master cast out devils? Moved with compassion, the Master beckoned the youth to him and took him by the hand. You know who I am, he said; come out of him. At once the young man was in his right mind. This was a genuine case of an evil spirit possessing a human being. Then another Pharisee stood and declared that the man could cast out devils because he was in league with them—had he not just admitted they knew each other? The teachers in Jerusalem, he said, had concluded that Jesus did all these things by the power of Beelzebub, the prince of devils.
ch10.b023: How could Satan cast out Satan? the Master asked. A kingdom divided against itself could not stand. And he gave a solemn warning to those who, with open eyes and premeditated malice, would knowingly put down the works of God to the doings of devils. Many of them, he said, stood today at the parting of the ways. A good tree bears good fruit. When yet another Pharisee asked him to agree beforehand on a sign that would prove his authority, the Master said that this faithless, sign-seeking generation would be given no sign except what it already had, and what it would see when the Son of Man departed from among them.
ch10.b024: When he had finished, the apostles closed around him and led him out of the synagogue. It was well past seven o’clock. All the way home to Bethsaida none of them said a word. Peter watched the Master’s back as he walked ahead. He had never before seen the Master speak like a man doing battle. At any other time he would have cheered to see it. Today it frightened him. He could not tell whom that back was fighting now, or where the fight would lead.
ch10.b026: When they reached home the Master would not eat. He went up to one of the upper rooms and stayed there alone for hours. No one downstairs dared go up. The twins covered the bread and fish left in the kitchen, so the Master could eat when he came down. They did it more than once—lifting the cloth to look, then covering it again.
ch10.b027: All evening loyal disciples came and went with news. Feeling in Capernaum had turned against the Master in a single evening. The men from Jerusalem were going from house to house urging people to keep away from him. Almost at midnight Joab, the leader of the young evangelists, came back—the same Joab who had led the clamor to crown the Master before the five thousand. About a third of his companions, he reported, had deserted. The twins heard this and looked at each other. A third. They were not quick with figures, but they knew that was a lot. The faces they had once lined up in rows and found places for—that many of them had vanished in a single night.
ch10.b028: The twins looked around at the others in the room. Simon Zelotes paced back and forth between the wall and the door. Again and again he started to say something and stopped. Thomas sat in a corner hugging his knees, saying nothing. The twins knew that when he was silent like that, it was best to leave him alone. Matthew was counting something on his fingers under the lamp. Nathaniel, for once, made no jokes. John sat on the bottom step of the stair that led to the upper room. He did not go up. He only sat there, in the place where he would be the first to know if the door opened. Philip was talking quietly with David about something, and Andrew looked from face to face, one after another. Peter sat with his back to the wall and his eyes closed. He was not asleep.
ch10.b029: At that same hour the twelve women were meeting at Peter’s house. They were all badly shaken. But none of them left. When the news reached the twins, one of them said quietly:
ch10.b031: “We’re not leaving either,” the other answered.
ch10.b032: He said it less like a resolution than like a plain fact. The thought of leaving simply had not occurred to them. Without crowds, the crowd-handlers would have nothing to do. That did not matter. If there was nothing else to do, they could cover the bread. There was a great deal the twins did not understand that night: what the bread of life was, why the Master had spoken as if in battle, why the people were going away. But they lost nothing.
ch10.b033: Judas Iscariot, sitting in a corner of the same room, heard that brief exchange. He could not tell whether he envied the twins or pitied them. They did not keep accounts, and so they had nothing to lose. He was a man who kept accounts. And tonight, for the first time, his accounts showed a loss. The numbers, the synagogue, the eyes of Jerusalem, the ears of Herod—not one line came out in their favor. He tried hard not to think of the drawer he had locked that afternoon in the synagogue.
ch10.b035: A little after midnight there were footsteps on the stair. The Master came down and stood among the twelve and their associates, about thirty in all. The lamplight wavered. His face was tired but composed. He knew, he told them, that this sifting of the kingdom distressed them, but it could not be avoided. After all their training, was there any good reason for them to stumble at his words? Why were they afraid as they watched the kingdom being stripped of these lukewarm crowds and halfhearted disciples? Why grieve, when a new day was dawning for the spiritual teachings of the kingdom to shine in new glory?
ch10.b036: If they found this test hard to bear, he asked, what would they do when the Son of Man had to return to the Father? It is the spirit that gives life, he said; the flesh profits little. The words he had spoken to them were spirit and life. They should take heart; he had not forsaken them. They had surely heard that many of his disciples had turned back and walked with him no more. He had known from the beginning that these halfhearted believers would fall away along the road.
ch10.b037: Then the Master looked around at them. One by one. Peter felt those eyes come to rest on him. Had he not chosen these twelve, the Master asked, and set them apart as ambassadors of the kingdom? At such a time as this, would they also leave? The room held nothing but the sound of breathing. And he added that each of them should examine his own faith, for one among them stood in grave danger.
ch10.b038: Peter drew a breath. Are you also so slow? The words still rang in his ears. The slow one. The one who had shouted king in the park a month ago. The one hauled out of the sea. All of it rose to his throat at once. And then something else rose above it. More than two years before, by the fire in Zebedee’s garden, he had said before his brothers that none of them would ever turn back. The warmth of that fire was still in his chest.
ch10.b039: Peter opened his mouth. His voice cracked. He did not try to steady it. Yes, Lord, he said, we are sad and perplexed, but we will never forsake you. The Master had taught them the words of eternal life. They had believed in him and followed him all this way. They would not turn back—for they knew he had been sent by God.
ch10.b040: When he had finished, they all nodded together, of one mind. Andrew nodded. John and James, Philip and Nathaniel, Thomas and Matthew, Simon Zelotes nodded. The twins nodded, hard, at the same moment. And Judas Iscariot nodded too. Peter saw it beyond the lamp and thought there was nothing strange about that nod. In truth there was nothing strange about it. Judas nodded sincerely. At least, at that moment, he believed he did.
ch10.b041: But the words “one of you” fell on Judas’s ear with a different weight. He swept his eyes quickly around the room. Who could it be? Peter, who had dreamed and walked into the sea? Simon, whose crown had been snatched away and who still carried a fire inside him? Or Thomas, the doubter? He did not put his own face among them. It did not even occur to him to try. That was Judas’s greatest talent: turning his eyes away from himself. He nodded, and with that nod he locked the drawer one more time.
ch10.b042: The Master looked at them for a long while and then told them to go and rest. Busy times were upon them; days of action lay just ahead. Peter could not sleep that night. He went out into the yard and sat for a long time looking at the dead hearth. Something red still glowed in the ashes. He held his hand to it. It was warm. He did not doubt what he had said that night. Only, for the first time, he began to feel a little of how heavy those words were.
ch10.b044: That same Saturday night, April 30, in Tiberias, Herod Antipas sat in council with special commissioners from the Sanhedrin. They urged him to arrest Jesus, insisting that he was stirring the people up. Herod refused. Chuza, of his own household—the husband of Joanna of the women’s corps—had already told him that Jesus had no intention of meddling in earthly government. Herod was also secretly haunted by fear over the killing of John the Baptist, and he did not want to be tangled up in another prophet’s affairs. When the Jews threatened to report him to Caesar, he ordered them out of his council chamber.
ch10.b045: From May 1 to May 7 the Master met morning, afternoon, and evening at Zebedee’s house with about a hundred trusted disciples—as many as had the courage to brave the Pharisees and openly declare themselves his followers. On the Friday, the rulers of the Capernaum synagogue shut the house of God against Jesus and all his followers. That day Jairus resigned as chief ruler and openly took the Master’s side. On the Sabbath afternoon, May 7, fewer than a hundred and fifty came to the last of the seaside meetings. That night marked the lowest ebb of the people’s regard. The next day, in Jerusalem, the Sanhedrin decreed that every synagogue in Palestine be closed to them. Within two weeks all but one had bowed to the decree; only the synagogue at Hebron refused.
ch10.b046: Judas Iscariot took in these reports one by one, as if entering them in his ledger. Each time a synagogue closed, something in him shrank by another notch. He could not stop counting. Every time Matthew went running about to fill the treasury, Judas sensed the money coming in more thinly than before. A man who had pushed away a crown before five thousand was now preaching to a hundred and fifty. What lay between the one and the other? A single word. The one word he had refused to say. To Judas it was not humility; it was waste.
ch10.b047: That same Sunday morning the Master declared a week of rest. They were each to go home, to play or to fish, and to pray for the kingdom. That week the Master went out fishing with David Zebedee several times, and two or three of David’s most trusted messengers always kept watch nearby without being seen. That was also the week Nathaniel and James Zebedee fell ill with a painful sickness of the stomach and lay for three days and nights. On the third night the Master sent James’s mother, Salome, who had been sitting up with them, off to rest, and nursed the two men himself. All night long he did not leave their bedside.
ch10.b048: Judas saw it from the doorway. The man who had opened a withered hand, who had raised the child they had thought dead, who had fed five thousand, was sitting up all night at the bedside of the sick. One word would have done it. And the Master did not say that word. Not even for his own. Judas could not understand it. Why was this man so unwilling to use his power? It was a question he had carried a long time. Tonight it set almost into certainty. He looked at Nathaniel’s pale face. The man who was always joking, the man who never seemed to take his apostleship seriously. And the Master was keeping watch beside him. Judas turned his back. What it was in him that stung, he could not have named exactly. Never once in all his life on earth did the Master work anything supernatural for his own family or his close followers. Judas never tried to learn why.
ch10.b049: On Saturday, May 21, just before midnight, Herod signed a decree in Tiberias allowing the officers of the Sanhedrin to seize Jesus in his domains and carry him to Jerusalem for trial. That same night, in the synagogue at Capernaum, fifty leading citizens argued until past midnight over what to do with him. A harmless fanatic, said some; a dangerous agitator, said others; in league with devils, said others again; or simply out of his mind. They never came to any agreement.
ch10.b051: On Sunday, May 22, before daybreak, one of David’s messengers came racing from Tiberias. Herod had authorized the arrest, or was about to. David roused his messengers and sent them out to every group of disciples with word of an emergency meeting at seven that morning. When Jude’s sister-in-law heard the news, she sent word to the Master’s family. Mary, James, Joseph, Jude, and Ruth set out.
ch10.b052: At that early meeting the Master gave his farewell instructions. Each of them was to seek God’s guidance and carry on the work of the kingdom whatever came. The evangelists were to work as they saw fit until they were called. He chose twelve of them to come with him. The twelve apostles he told to stay with him no matter what happened. The twelve women were to remain at Zebedee’s house and Peter’s house until he sent for them. David Zebedee said he would keep his messenger service going; he had already named a first, a second, even a third leader, so that whatever happened to him the work would not stop. He was neither teacher nor preacher, he said, but this was in his heart to do, and no one could stop him.
ch10.b053: At about half past seven the Master began his parting address to nearly a hundred believers crowded into the house. It was a solemn occasion. Yet the Master was more cheerful than he had been in weeks. The heaviness of his face was gone, and words of faith and hope and courage poured from him. Seeing that face hurt Peter more than anything. A man who could be so bright on the morning he was being hunted. Peter could not understand it, but he wanted to lean on that light.
ch10.b054: Around eight o’clock there was a stir at the back porch. People who could not get into the packed house were gathered there. A message passed from person to person. The last to receive it was Peter. He went to the Master and whispered in his ear: his mother and his brothers were outside, and they were very anxious to speak with him. Peter was glad as he passed it on. The family had come. On this hunted morning, his mother had come. The Master would surely stop speaking and go to them at once, he thought. Mary must have thought so too.
ch10.b055: The Master paused for a moment. Then he spoke more loudly, in a voice that reached every corner of the room. Tell my mother and my brothers, he said, not to be afraid for me. The Father who sent him would not forsake him, and no harm would come to his family. Let them take courage and trust the Father. But who, after all, was his mother, and who were his brothers? He stretched out his hands toward the disciples gathered in the room. He had no mother, he said, and no brothers—look, here were his mother and his brothers. Whoever did the will of his Father in heaven was his mother, his brother, his sister.
ch10.b056: The twins saw his hands pass over them. They took the words just as they were spoken. My brothers. Two fishermen who had never finished synagogue school, two men who had been covering bread with a cloth only that morning. One twin gripped the other’s arm hard. They did not think how those words would sound to a woman standing on the back porch. They were simply glad. That was their blessing, and that morning the blessing hurt a little.
ch10.b057: On the back porch, Mary heard the words. She collapsed into the arms of her son Jude. They carried her into the garden to revive her. Through a gap in the door Peter saw the commotion. It was he who had carried her message in. He bit his lip. The Master finished the last words of his farewell. And then he meant to go out to his family.
ch10.b058: At that moment another messenger came running from Tiberias: the officers of the Sanhedrin were on their way to arrest him. Andrew took the message and broke in on the Master to tell him. He had forgotten that David had posted some twenty-five sentinels around the house. What should they do? he asked. The Master stood silent, while in the garden his mother was coming to herself. Just then a woman in the room stood up and cried out that blessed was the womb that had borne him and the breasts that had nursed him. The Master turned from Andrew to answer her. No, he said; rather blessed is the one who hears the word of God and dares to obey it.
ch10.b059: At that very moment a party of David’s messengers came bursting in at the back door. The commotion threw the apostles into a panic. They thought the officers had arrived. They surrounded the Master, swept him out through the front door, and ran for the waiting boat. And so the Master never saw his family waiting on the back porch. As he stepped into the boat, he told David to tell his mother and brothers that he was grateful they had come and that he had meant to see them. They were not to take offense at him, he said, but to seek to know the will of God, and the grace and courage to do it.
ch10.b061: It was nearly half past eight when the boat pulled away from the shore: the Master, the twelve apostles, and the twelve evangelists, twenty-five in all. It was a beautiful morning. The water was still and the sky was blue. A smaller boat followed them, carrying six of David’s messengers, who were to keep word of the Master’s whereabouts flowing back to Bethsaida. On the shore a crowd stood watching the two boats grow smaller toward the east. Only after that did the officers from Jerusalem come hurrying up, out of breath.
ch10.b062: Judas Iscariot had an oar. With every stroke the purse at his belt knocked against his side. It was light. He looked back. Zebedee’s big house was growing smaller—the house that had been the headquarters of the kingdom for so long, the shore where the tented city had stood, the room into which the paralytic had been lowered through the roof. Judas totted it all up. And he looked at what was left at the bottom of the sum. Two boats. Twenty-five men. One man with nowhere to lay his head. That was where the bread for five thousand had brought them, in less than two months.
ch10.b063: He thought of Jericho. The money he had deposited in that bank. On the day the apostolic purse first had something to spare, he had taken it as a sign that the kingdom was growing. The money was still there. But the kingdom that was to spend it was now in a boat, fleeing. Judas drove his oar in deep. Water splashed. He thought of the drawer he had locked in the synagogue. I could leave this man. The sentence lifted its head again. This time more easily, more quietly. He pressed it down once more. Not yet. Who could say what the Master would do at the very end? Only, he did not notice that his hand pressed down with less force than before.
ch10.b064: Near the bow sat Peter, close beside the Master, gazing at the eastern shore. Last night’s words were still in his mouth. We will not turn back. This morning he understood a little more of what they meant. Turning your back on your house, on your family on the shore, getting into a boat while the Master’s mother lay fainted in the garden. He tried not to look back. In the end he looked back once. Somewhere on the shore at Bethsaida were his wife and his children. He faced forward again. The Master’s profile was bright in the morning sun.
ch10.b065: The twins sat side by side, rowing in the same rhythm. They did not know where they were going. They did not ask. There were no crowds, so there were no crowds to handle. There were oars instead. That was enough for them. One twin said over again the words from that morning: my brothers. The other nodded. At the same moment, both their hearts grew warm. The boat pulled on toward Kheresa, toward that steep shore where once the swine had gone tumbling into the sea.
ch10.b066: Andrew, at the stern, counted the company. Twenty-five. No one was missing. His eyes rested for a moment on Judas’s back as he rowed. The back was straight. His stroke was exact. There was nothing to fault. And yet the words the Master had spoken the night before still troubled Andrew. One of you. He did not know who it was. He only kept it in mind. And he said nothing to anyone.
ch10.b067: From that morning on, the Master never again made his home in Zebedee’s house. For the rest of his days on earth he truly had nowhere to lay his head. While the Pharisees spent almost a whole week searching for him in vain around Capernaum, the company passed into Philip’s domains and went north. On the Thursday afternoon of that week, Ruth, the Master’s sister, came to Zebedee’s house and heard from David that her brother was safe and well and making his way toward the coast of Phoenicia; only then could the family breathe again. To those left on the shore, all that remained was that one line of news. To those in the boat, all that remained was one another.
ch10.b069: The events follow Papers 153 and 154: the apostles on the eve and morning of the synagogue sermon and what each said, Judas Iscariot’s thought, and the greeting of one of the twins (153:0.1–0.3); the Jerusalem delegation and Herod’s observers in the synagogue, and Jairus’s reply (153:1.1–1.7); the readings from Deuteronomy and Jeremiah, the sermon on the bread of life, the carved pot of manna, and the Sanhedrist’s question (153:2.1–2.13); Judas’s first conscious thought of deserting after this sermon, and his mastering of it (153:1.5); the questions of the after meeting, Peter’s question, the possessed youth, the Beelzebub charge, and the demand for a sign (153:3.1–4.6); the upper room, Joab’s report, the women at Peter’s house, the midnight talk, and Peter’s pledge (153:5.1–5.5); the council of Herod and the Sanhedrin at Tiberias and Chuza’s report (154:0.1–0.3); the week of conferences, the closing of the synagogue, Jairus’s resignation, and the last seaside meeting (154:1.1–1.3); the Sanhedrin’s decree and Hebron, the week of rest, the illness of Nathaniel and James, and Jesus’s nursing of them (154:2.1–2.4); Herod’s signature (154:3.1–3.2); the four views of the Capernaum citizens (154:4.1–4.5); the news of May 22, the farewell instructions, David’s words, the family’s visit and Jesus’s reply, Mary’s collapse, the woman’s cry, the hasty departure, and the message left with David (154:5.1–6.12); and the boat of twenty-five, the messengers’ boat, the crossing toward Kheresa, and Ruth’s news (154:7.1–7.5).
ch10.b070: Character details are drawn from Paper 139 and elsewhere: Judas’s belief that Jesus was timid about using his power, and his habit of self-deception (139:12.4–12.9); Judas’s grievance against Nathaniel (139:6.5); Peter’s swings of feeling and his loyalty (139:2.3–2.6); the twins’ simplicity and their management of the crowds (139:9.2–9.8); Andrew’s early sense of trouble in Judas, which he told to no one (139:1.8); and the deposit at Jericho (147:2.1).
ch10.b071: Added fiction includes the characters’ inner thoughts and feelings (the image of Judas locking his thought in a drawer, the way Judas and Andrew received the words “one of you,” Peter’s memory of the fire in the garden and his remorse over Mary); sensory detail of the synagogue, the night, and the morning sea; the twins sweeping the yard and covering the bread, and their brief exchange; how each apostle waited beneath the upper room; Judas’s irritation at Nathaniel’s remark; and the thoughts of Judas, Peter, the twins, and Andrew in the boat. The text does not say which twin gave the greeting, so it is left unnamed. Where Judas’s trouble and Peter’s pledge will lead is left to later chapters.
ch10.b072: The words of Jesus are retold, not quoted, following the sense of the text.
